evidence.title: Russell Herman, Greens Functions and Nonhomogeneous Problems
evidence.finding: The source-integral Green representation uses homogeneous boundary conditions; prescribed nonhomogeneous data require their additional solution contribution.
The difference between two fundamental solutions for the same point source is homogeneous away from singular support; boundary data select the needed correction where a Green problem is well posed.
Nullspaces and Neumann compatibility can prevent uniqueness or require normalization; boundary data do not guarantee an invertible operator in every problem.

evidence.title: Waterloo CS370, Numerical computation notes, pp.104–105
evidence.finding: The implicit trapezoidal method averages endpoint slopes, giving the standard second-order update.
y_(n+1)=y_n+(h/2)*(f(t_n,y_n)+f(t_(n+1),y_(n+1))) averages endpoint slopes and is second order under smoothness.

Averaging Euler means the endpoint slope formulas, not averaging two independently completed step solutions. It is A-stable for the linear test problem but not L-stable and can retain stiff oscillations.

records.rationale: Sine and cosine are not eigenfunctions of the first-derivative operator as stated. Differentiation sends sine to cosine and cosine to negative sine rather than a constant multiple of itself.

evidence.finding: Each algebraic, differential, transform, probability and counterexample calculation is independently checked.

evidence.title: MIT 18.06, Operators
evidence.finding: Differentiation maps sine to cosine and cosine to negative sine; they are eigenfunctions of second differentiation, not first differentiation.
D sin x=cos x cannot equal lambda*sin x for allx, since at0 the left side is1 and the right side0. Both are eigenfunctions of D² with eigenvalue-1; exp(±i*x) are eigenfunctions ofD.
Their importance in wave/heat problems is valid, but replacing differentiation with second differentiation would rewrite the incorrect source claim.
